title: Choosing between a Spark session and a Python notebook in Fabric
purpose: Engine choice between Spark and Python notebooks. Working data size heuristic; Python notebook path; Small Spark session path; Scaled Spark pool path; Overrides that beat size; Maintenance consequence.
accessibleSummary: Engine choice between Spark and Python notebooks. Working data size heuristic; Python notebook path; Small Spark session path; Scaled Spark pool path; Overrides that beat size; Maintenance consequence.
longDescription: Engine choice between Spark and Python notebooks. Working data size heuristic; Python notebook path; Small Spark session path; Scaled Spark pool path; Overrides that beat size; Maintenance consequence.

nodes.label: Under roughly 5–10 GB
nodes.summary: Under roughly 5-10 GB a single-node Python notebook is usually the cheaper answer.
nodes.detail: Under roughly 5-10 GB a single-node Python notebook is usually the cheaper answer.
nodes.whyItMatters: Under roughly 5-10 GB a single-node Python notebook is usually the cheaper answer.

evidence.note: Under roughly 5-10 GB of working data a single-node Python notebook with Polars, DuckDB or delta-rs is usually the cheaper answer.

processing: Run single-node with a vectorized engine
outputs: Results at a fraction of the capacity cost
drill.example: A daily reference-data refresh runs in a Python notebook in seconds rather than starting a Spark cluster.
failureModes: The threshold is a heuristic; a memory-hungry transform can exceed a single node well below it.

nodes.label: Roughly 10–100 GB
nodes.summary: Between roughly 10 and 100 GB a small Spark session fits without wide-cluster shuffles.
nodes.detail: Between roughly 10 and 100 GB a small Spark session fits without wide-cluster shuffles.
nodes.whyItMatters: Between roughly 10 and 100 GB a small Spark session fits without wide-cluster shuffles.

evidence.note: Roughly 10-100 GB suits a small Spark session.
Fabric Spark pools offer selectable node sizes for the workload.

processing: Run a small Spark session with native execution enabled
outputs: Distributed processing without a wide cluster
drill.example: A silver conform job runs on two or three Medium nodes rather than a large pool.
failureModes: Over-provisioning at this size wastes capacity units without reducing runtime.

nodes.label: Beyond roughly 100 GB with joins
nodes.summary: Beyond roughly 100 GB with real joins, a scaled Spark pool is warranted.
nodes.detail: Beyond roughly 100 GB with real joins, a scaled Spark pool is warranted.
nodes.whyItMatters: Beyond roughly 100 GB with real joins, a scaled Spark pool is warranted.

evidence.note: Beyond roughly 100 GB with real joins and shuffles a scaled Spark pool is warranted.
Efficient Scaledown decouples shuffle data from executor lifetime so nodes can be released.

inputs: Large working sets with joins and shuffles
processing: Size the pool from shuffle volume
drill.example: A gold aggregation over a multi-terabyte silver table sizes its pool from shuffle volume, not input size.
failureModes: Sizing from input volume rather than shuffle volume under-provisions the expensive stage.

nodes.label: Gold writes for Direct Lake
nodes.summary: Gold writes for Direct Lake belong in Spark because delta-rs cannot apply V-Order.
nodes.detail: Gold writes for Direct Lake belong in Spark because delta-rs cannot apply V-Order.
nodes.whyItMatters: Gold writes for Direct Lake belong in Spark because delta-rs cannot apply V-Order.

evidence.note: Writes destined for Direct Lake gold should go through Spark because delta-rs cannot apply V-Order.
V-Order is a write-time optimization that improves read performance for Direct Lake and the SQL endpoint.

inputs: A gold table serving Direct Lake or the SQL endpoint
processing: Write from Spark so V-Order applies
drill.example: A small gold aggregate is still written from Spark so Direct Lake reads stay fast.
failureModes: A Python-written gold table loses V-Order and degrades Direct Lake read performance.

nodes.label: Genuinely distributed shuffles
nodes.summary: Genuinely distributed shuffles are Spark territory regardless of input size.
nodes.detail: Genuinely distributed shuffles are Spark territory regardless of input size.
nodes.whyItMatters: Genuinely distributed shuffles are Spark territory regardless of input size.

evidence.note: Anything needing a genuinely distributed shuffle is Spark territory regardless of input size.

drill.example: A join between two large fact tables cannot be done single-node whatever the file sizes suggest.
failureModes: Attempting a distributed join single-node exhausts memory rather than running slowly.

nodes.label: Why this is the expensive mistake
nodes.summary: Using a multi-node Spark session for single-node work is the most expensive common mistake.
nodes.detail: Using a multi-node Spark session for single-node work is the most expensive common mistake.
nodes.whyItMatters: Using a multi-node Spark session for single-node work is the most expensive common mistake.

evidence.note: The most expensive Fabric Spark mistake is running a multi-node Spark session for work a single small node could do.

processing: Compare capacity cost against the work actually required
drill.example: A dozen small daily jobs each starting a Spark pool consume far more capacity than the work justifies.
controls: Engine choice per entity in a metadata-driven framework
failureModes: The cost is invisible per job and only obvious in aggregate capacity consumption.

nodes.label: Python-written tables need more maintenance
nodes.summary: Tables written from the Python kernel receive no auto-compaction and need more maintenance.
nodes.detail: Tables written from the Python kernel receive no auto-compaction and need more maintenance.
nodes.whyItMatters: Tables written from the Python kernel receive no auto-compaction and need more maintenance.

evidence.note: Tables written from the Python kernel get no auto-compaction and VACUUM never runs automatically, so they need more maintenance, not less.

inputs: Tables written from the Python kernel
drill.example: A Python-written bronze table accumulates small files until an explicit OPTIMIZE runs.
failureModes: Choosing Python for cost and skipping maintenance trades compute saving for scan cost later.

edges.label: Growing working set moves up a band
Shuffle volume moves up a band
Direct Lake gold writes force Spark
Distributed joins force a scaled pool
Python-kernel writes carry a maintenance cost
